rows.en: These several proofs will show that the method of interpreting the Torah was insight into the reasons of the statutes and reflection on their spiritual purpose. This also follows from all the religious traces that we have in the writings composed in the time of Solomon, whether he himself was the writer or one of the men of his generation, or that were written in the generations after him and speak of his affairs; so much so that we can almost say that these writings are the most correct interpretations of the statutes of the Torah. Let us consider here what their view was regarding the worship of God in the Temple. Just as we saw that already in the eyes of Samuel the sacrificial service had worth and value only as a means to attaining a moral goal, so, and with even greater force, this appears from the writings and the sayings attributed to Solomon or speaking from sources of his time. What in Solomon's eyes was the purpose of the house that he built, and what was its function? Was it to be only a house of sacrifice{v1_03_05:2} and no more? If we pay attention to the prayer that he prayed, we find that in his eyes the function of the house was to be an open spring for the house of Israel, from which would issue the sources of life for the spirit of religion. This house would gather the hearts of the individuals of the nation like sheaves to the threshing floor, and from there God's providence would go forth over the nation as a whole and over its individuals in particular. And in all the deeds that he did on that occasion, it appears that his conception of religion rose above material attributes; therefore the worship of God that Solomon established had no other purpose than to bring his people to a true knowledge of the God of their fathers and to unite all Israel at one point. So much for the worship of God in general! As for the sacrificial service, they did not depart from the way that Samuel had paved before them. It is true that both David and Solomon held to the sacrificial service as Moses commanded, but the service was very, very evil in their eyes if it was done according to the views of the multitude, who thought that only the outward act is what God desires; just as the matter was evil in the eyes of the prophets of their time and after them. Who was more zealous against the outward service in sacrifices than David in his psalms and Solomon in his proverbs? In clear words David declares his view: that God has no desire for sacrifice and offering, and has not asked for burnt offering and sin offering (Psalms 40:7). And another of the poets of his time also speaks in this direction, saying: that only then is the sacrifice acceptable to God if the one who sacrifices makes the covenant of the Lord over the sacrifice; God will not accept burnt offering and sacrifice, but He will accept a thanksgiving sacrifice which will be a sign of the feelings of his heart, for only by a thanksgiving sacrifice does he honor God (ibid. 50). And this same spirit hovers also over Solomon's words in his Proverbs. He too says that God does not desire the sacrifices of the wicked, and they are an abomination if they are brought with evil intent (Proverbs 21:27), and that to do justice and righteousness is more acceptable to the Lord than sacrifice (ibid. 21:3). And in the song that was sung for the glory of the dedication of the House, the one who ascends the mountain of the Lord to stand in His holy place is not asked to multiply his sacrifices and the cattle on a thousand hills, but is asked for clean hands and a pure heart, that he not lift up his soul to vanity nor swear deceitfully (Psalms 25:3, 4).⚠1 And if we look further at the psalms and songs that were sung when the tribes of the Lord went up to see the face of the Lord God three times a year, the root and reason of this statute also emerge for us from their content and from the idea that governs them: that the chief cause and purpose of the pilgrimage was, first and foremost, nothing other than to awaken and arouse in them national love and to strengthen the holy bond that unites all the individuals of the nation. The assemblies of the tribes of the Lord will be a testimony to Israel. And Jerusalem, which is the place of holiness, for there is the house of the Lord and there sat the thrones of the house of David, is itself the point from which this union goes forth. Therefore who will not ask after its peace? Will not all who love it prosper in its peace? And who will not speak peace in it for the sake of the brothers and companions who are joined in it soul to soul? (ibid. 122). And ideas like these emerge for us from all the songs that were composed to be sung as they went up to see the face of the Lord God in Jerusalem. And if it is said, "and they shall not appear before Me empty" [Exodus 23:15], and Deuteronomy states explicitly, "every man shall give as he is able, according to the blessing of the Lord thy God which He hath given thee" [Deuteronomy 16:17], this is not the main reason but a secondary condition. Now we will see how great the idea of this statute was according to the understanding of the early time, and how small, in comparison, its intention was according to what is described by the later ones in the days of the Second Temple, who already took the secondary as the main thing and applied petty niceties to it. And so we see in all this correct interpretations, and we rightly say that all the writings from that time and after it are the most correct interpretations of the statutes of the Torah.

1.note: The verses quoted are Psalm 24:3-4; the print has 25.

rows.en: One foundation which has no source except in the oral tradition came into being in the course of this period. This foundation is the hope for the revelation of the King Messiah. Many have sought the source of this hope in the Torah of Moses. But they erred in vision, and the matter is not so, for it cannot be. If we unroll before us the sublime visions that depict the face of the time in which this hope will be fulfilled, then we will see that its foundation is not in the Torah of Moses, and that by its nature it is not even possible to seek its foundation in the Torah and in the time of the nation's childhood. The moral perfection of all human society through the Israelite nation, which will raise the banner of the knowledge of the true God to all the peoples; a kingdom of God led by the hand of a human king of the seed of Judah; the flourishing of truth and uprightness, peace, love, general happiness, the knowledge of God and the fear of Him: these are the signs that mark the face of that time as the prophets described it. And where in the Torah of Moses is there even one hint of all these? And how can we search the Torah for a source for a hope of establishing a human kingdom, when according to the law and the will of the Torah there is to be in Israel only the kingdom of Heaven and no human king?{v1_03_06:1} And even if we say that according to the Torah too a human kingdom was within the bounds of the possible, still how could it enter our mind that the Torah would set up a thing that is against its will as the model of their hope and of their final national goal? Moreover, it plainly follows from the Torah of Moses that its intention was to implant in them the thought that they are a treasure among all the peoples and that their function is to be separate from the nations in their character, their statutes and their customs; and in the time of the nation's childhood this was very necessary, out of concern lest they mingle with the nations and learn their deeds. How then could it enter the mind that at that time it was proclaimed in the nation that one kingdom would be in the land, shared by Israel and all the nations together? (See Luzzatto in his commentary on Isaiah 2:5.) But let us see what are the traces in which, in their view, this hope is laid down. First, they hint at the general promises, some of them to the patriarchs (Genesis 17:4-7; 22:18; 26:4; 25:14;⚠1 35:11) and some to the nation itself (Leviticus 26:44, and in Deuteronomy in many places). But who does not know that all these promises are no more than general assurances that the Lord will keep His covenant with them, and that they have nothing to do with the hope of the Messiah? Only in Deuteronomy is it said, in a slight hint, that the function of the nation is also to be a banner to the nations: "and all the peoples of the earth shall see that the name of the Lord is called upon them,⚠2 and they shall be afraid of them" (Deuteronomy 28:10). But this too is very far from what the prophets describe of the hope of the Messiah. It is true that promises speaking of a particular individual are also hinted at. One is what is said in the blessing of Jacob: "The scepter shall not depart from Judah, nor the ruler's staff from between his feet, until Shiloh come, and unto him shall the obedience of the peoples be" (Genesis 49:8).⚠3 Many have wished to find in this promise a hint of the Messiah. One explains "until the man comes to whom the kingdom belongs" (Genesis Rabbah 99), or "he to whom they bring a gift [shai lo]" (*Yalkut*, remez 160); another says that Shiloh is a proper name of the Messiah (Sanhedrin 98b); and others say that Shiloh is like "Prince of Peace" [Isaiah 9:5], which is an epithet of the Messiah (Rosenmüller, Hengstenberg). See how weak this idea would be if it had no other foundation than such poor niceties. And it is very clear that among the ancients the word Shiloh was not expounded as referring to the Messiah; for if it were so, why did they not choose the name Shiloh to call the Messiah by, since it would be the epithet given him in the Torah? And if we explain the words according to their meaning and their true plain sense, far from the ways of midrash, it will become clear to us that the Torah did not think of hinting at the kingdom of the Messiah, but set before its eyes the function of the tribe of Judah at different times. For until they came to Shiloh, Judah went at the head of all the men of war in the conquest of the land; from the days of the Judges onward its dominion was held back, until the kingship came to David, "and unto him shall the obedience of the peoples be": not only all the tribes, who are also called peoples, but other peoples too served him and were placed under his rule. Therefore, whoever wishes to expound this saying of the Torah as referring to the Messiah by way of midrash or aggadic figure of speech, we say: leave him be, for great is the license given to every preacher. But to one who says that this is truly the intention of the Torah, we say that he errs and leads others astray. One of Balaam's prophecies too was expounded as referring to the Messiah. It is what he said: "I see him, but not now; I behold him, but not nigh; there shall step forth a star out of Jacob, and a scepter shall rise out of Israel, and shall smite through the corners of Moab, and break down all the sons of Seth. And Edom shall be a possession, Seir also shall be a possession, while Israel doeth valiantly" (Numbers 24:17-18). But anyone who has eyes will see that these words are aimed at the kingdom of David, for he was the man who smote through the corners of Moab and broke down all its helpers; he made Edom a possession, "and all Edom became servants to him" (2 Samuel 9);⚠4 and these peoples and their helpers were the sons of Seth, or the sons of tumult [she'on] (Jeremiah 48), whom he would break down, and did break down. And how could it enter the mind that their hope of enlarging the border in the days of the kingdom of the Messiah was only for the conquest of Moab and Edom and no more? Were not the borders of the Land of Israel enlarged still further at various times, as in the days of Solomon and also in the days of John Hyrcanus I, and still they hoped for the Messiah who would come? Indeed this error of expounding these verses as referring to a Messiah grew only from their seeing that R. Akiva expounded the verse "there shall step forth a star out of Jacob" as referring to Bar Kokhba, whom they held to be the Messiah. But who does not know that R. Akiva did not think to explain the verse; rather he expounded it by way of aggadah, as a play on words, to arouse the heart of the people, in the manner of preachers? But in truth the sages of the Talmud too did not think to rest the foundations of this hope, as it is described in the prophets, upon the Torah, since they knew that it is not found in it and its root is not in the Torah. Therefore we do not find that they ask anywhere, "Where in the Torah is the coming of the Messiah derived from?", as they ask in several places concerning the resurrection of the dead. Rather, the foundations on which this hope was built were the kingdom of David. Already in the days of David the idea took root in the nation that its function is to be an example to all the peoples, so that they too would learn to fear the Lord and to recognize that the Lord is one God and there is none beside Him. David's own heart was full of this great idea, and he sang of it in his psalms, in his hope: "Nobles shall come out of Egypt; Cush shall hasten to stretch out her hands unto God; ye kingdoms of the earth, sing unto Him" (Psalms 68:32, 33). And with still greater force this idea found its place in the song attributed to him, which he sang when he set the ark of God inside the tent (1 Chronicles 106:23-34; Psalms 96, 96).⚠5 The reign of David was the most exalted and the happiest of the reigns of all the kings of Israel in every respect. The political situation, the abundance of good and happiness in the land, and likewise the moral situation and the spread of knowledge and the fear of the Lord, stood at a level whose like had not been before him nor after him among all the kings. And when they saw that the moral state was very high and lofty, and that the tree of knowledge and the Torah grew and bore fruit, and when they saw that bound up with this their political success too was flourishing and their heritage very fair, this was a testimony to them that the height of their moral state is also the cause of their temporal success, and that because of it the happiness they had been promised of old reached them. And since David had raised them to this state, they therefore saw that the continuance of this happy state, and its rising from strength to strength in the future, was bound to David and his kingdom and would never be separated from it. This idea was strengthened by the prophets, who prophesied so in the name of the Lord. In particular Nathan the prophet poured strong confidence into David's heart when he said: "And thy house and thy kingdom shall be made sure for ever; thy throne shall be established for ever" (2 Samuel 7:16). Such promises were repeated many times, as we see from David's last words to his son Solomon, when he handed on to him such a promise that he had received in the name of the Lord: "There shall not fail thee a man on the throne of Israel" (1 Kings 2:4). These assurances sank deep into the chambers of David's heart, in his hope that the Lord would make great His salvation and show kindness to His anointed, to David and to his seed for ever. Yet, like every great idea that in its childhood is not yet clear, because opinions have not yet been purified, and reveals itself only little by little until it shines forth in its strength, so it was with the idea of the perfecting of the world through the kingdom of the house of David, which already at the beginning of Solomon's reign began to reveal itself with greater force. In clear words Solomon speaks of this perfecting when he prays to the Lord that He fulfil the requests of the stranger who will pray in His sanctuary, "that all the peoples of the earth may know Thy name, to fear Thee, as do Thy people Israel" (1 Kings 8){v1_03_08:1} and "that all the peoples of the earth may know that the Lord, He is God; there is none else" (ibid. 9).⚠6 The desire that all these good things be fulfilled, and that all the wishes of his heart come true in the future, was the reason that Solomon strove to show the peoples the wisdom that flows from the source of the Lord's religion; and his desire also prospered in his hand, for the fame of his wisdom went forth for the name of the Lord (ibid. 10:1). And what was this wisdom? Not the wisdom of the children of the East, of Tyre and Sidon, Canaan and its borders; not the wisdom of Egypt, Cush and Babylon and their regions, all of whose wisdom came to naught in the course of time; but his wisdom was a wisdom that will never be removed. For the contemplation of the sublime sights in the nature of created things, the contemplation of man in his moral qualities, and the contemplation of God's providence as seen in the history of man in particular and of the nations of the world in general: this was his wisdom. And from where was this wisdom taken? From the Torah of Moses in the first place, and from the teachings of the prophets and of the sages of the generations and their poets. The spirit that was in these was not a spirit of vanity from the vanities of the nations; therefore it was not a passing spirit but one that stands and endures and is fitting for all times and for all mankind together. With wisdom like this Solomon could hope that it would find lovers among the peoples and would win their hearts, to bring them into the covenant of the Lord. These ideas are written by the hand of the poets of the time in their songs of praise. In the song that was sung in honor of Solomon on the day he came to the throne, the poet speaks in praise of the king and depicts him in the excellence of righteousness and justice in his judgment of the poor of his people: that he will save the children of the needy and crush the oppressor; for his sake the mountains will bear peace to the people as long as the moon endures; he shall have dominion from sea to sea and from the River to the ends of the earth; before him the desert-dwellers will bow, all kings shall prostrate themselves before him, all nations shall serve him; there shall be abundance of grain in the land upon the top of the mountains, its fruit shall rustle like Lebanon, and they of the city shall blossom like grass of the field; his name shall endure for ever, and all nations shall be blessed in him and call him happy (Psalms 72). And if we consider this picture, here before us is the picture in its completeness, as the prophets describe the King Messiah, his time and his kingdom. It is indeed true that the kingdom of David is the foundation of the hope of the Messiah. But the first point of the beginning of this hope was not in the time of David or of Solomon. For, according to what we have seen, the kingdom of the house of David was the sublime picture in whose likeness they hoped for the kingdom of the King Messiah. And it is self-evident that during David's reign there was no room for such a hope, since the hoped-for kingdom was present in actuality, and what would hope do? Rather, the hope of the Messiah began to sprout when the success of the kingdom went backward; for so it lies in the nature of things: when the good is lost, we seek comfort in the hope that the days to come will bring it back to us and will be better than the present. Already in Solomon's last days signs of decline were evident in his kingdom. For the ways in which Solomon went to achieve the mission of Israel⚠7 were not the right ways. He favored the peoples of the land who were his servants and gave them leave to act according to the law of their religion, hoping that in the course of time they would turn and recognize the true religion. But the opposite happened, for the abominations of the nations became a snare to him and to his people. He increased the glory of his house with outward splendor, thinking to exalt his kingdom by this, but this was his undoing, for under the pressure of the taxes and his heavy yoke the people were crushed and the strength of their endurance failed; therefore his kingdom did not continue over all Israel. In the days of his son Rehoboam, who erred in his father's errors and did even worse than he, the kingdom was already divided. And because of this they moved far away from the goal. The confidence they had placed in the continuance of the house of David came to nothing. Before two generations had passed, their political and moral success had passed away into nothing; and in such a time the longing to restore what had been lost grows, and it is the mother of the hope that the good will return in the future; and in the evil blows to the kingdom they saw only a temporary delay, not eternal despair. Therefore in this evil time the hope of the Messiah began to sprout. And we rightly say that the reign of David was the quarry from which the stones were hewn to build the palace of the sublime idea of the revelation of the kingdom of the Messiah. Two generations after this the first stone of its foundation was laid in Zion; and builders labored to complete the building of the palace in all the generations that came, setting stone upon stone. The house was one in its form and structure from outside, but its structure within and all its inner parts changed time after time, according to the change of the spirit of the time, according to the prevailing concepts, and also according to the demands that the time made. Therefore its completion to the end is still wrapped from our eyes in the darkness of distant times⚠8 that are yet to come, and it is to us today still a hidden riddle. And this riddle is one with the great and hidden secret of the goal of the development of enlightenment, of the life of society and of the justice of law, of morality and of faith, for all the multitude of mankind together.

footnotes.en: This idea is laid down⚠1 also in Scripture in another place. That is, when the author of Chronicles describes the reason why the Lord withheld from him the building of the Temple, he puts his words in the mouth of David, who speaks in the name of the Lord and says: "Thou hast shed blood abundantly ... thou shalt not build a house unto My name" (1 Chronicles 27:7).⚠2

footnotes.en: In 1 Kings 8:65-66: "And Solomon held the feast at that time ... seven days and seven days, even fourteen days. On the eighth day he sent the people away." And in 1 Chronicles⚠1 (7:8-10): "And Solomon held the feast at that time seven days ... And on the eighth day they made a solemn assembly, for they kept the dedication of the altar seven days, and the feast seven days. And on the three and twentieth day of the seventh month he sent the people away." How are we to understand this? For according to one version he sent the people away on the eighth day, and according to the other the eighth day was the solemn assembly. And according to the version in Kings the feast was exactly fourteen days, and how could this be? Necessarily, as we wrote in the text, the festival of consecration began with special intention on the ninth of the month; therefore the festival, that is, the first seven days, ended on the fifteenth of the month, and that was already the first day of Sukkot; and there remained for Sukkot together with Shemini Atzeret only seven days, and on the eighth day after these seven days he sent the people away, and that was the twenty-third of the seventh month. And only in this way can these two verses be reconciled, which as they appear to our eyes contradict each other.

footnotes.en: If the narrator in Chronicles says that it was said to Solomon in the visions of the night, "I have heard thy prayer, and have chosen this place to Myself for a house of sacrifice" (2 Chronicles 8:12),⚠1 this is only because the author of Chronicles depicted the matter according to the views of his own time; but in the narrative in Kings, which is founded on primary and old sources, there is no mention of this.
See the *History of the People of Israel* by the scholar Ewald, part 3, p. 146.

The prayer placed in Solomon's mouth (1 Kings 8) is for the most part only attributed to him by a later writer; so the majority of recent critics agree. In my opinion the core of the prayer that may truly be attributed to Solomon is: from verse 23 to 26, 28 to 30, 41 to 43. One should also remark here on my attributing Psalm 68 to David. This is because in any case it was written before the kingdom was divided, as appears from verse 28. And since it mentions much of the strength and the salvation that they had against the enemy, this shows that the song was sung at some time when they returned from war in victory and strength, and this is not possible in the days of Solomon. But on this view there is a difficulty in that verse 30 speaks of a temple over Jerusalem, while even at the end of David's days there was in Jerusalem only an altar for burnt offering? But in 1 Chronicles 21:31⚠1 he calls it "the house of the Lord God." See on this the commentary on Psalms by the scholar De Wette.⚠2 The ending of the song, verse 37, seems to be a later addition, as in my opinion they did in several psalms. For the psalms were sung in the Temple, and they sometimes made additions for the needs of their time. See Psalm 51:20, 21, and ibid. 72:18, 19, and in several other places.

1.note: 1 Chronicles 21 has 30 verses; 'the house of the Lord God' is at 22:1.

2.note: Name unclear in print; taken as De Wette.
